sections.1.heading: Choosing time tracking software for UK businesses
sections.1.body:
Choosing **time tracking software for UK businesses** starts with a simple question: what is the tracking for? The answer decides which kind of tool you need, and the UK has a few specific points worth knowing for each.

| What you need | Kind of tool | UK point to know |
|---|---|---|
| Bill clients for hours | Billable time tracker | Rates in sterling or the client's currency; VAT on invoices |
| Record shifts for payroll | Clock-in and attendance tool | Working time rules and pay records |
| Watch computer activity | Monitoring tool | Data protection guidance on monitoring workers |

Paidlyo is the first kind. It's built for agencies, studios, consultancies and freelancers who bill clients by the hour. Everyone tracks time against a client, a project and a task, with a timer or a weekly timesheet. Rates are set per project or task, and invoices are built from unbilled hours.

It isn't a clock-in system, a payroll tool or a monitoring tool. If your main need is recording shift times for hourly-paid staff, an attendance tool linked to payroll will suit you better. If your main need is knowing how many billable hours went into each client, read on.

Many UK firms also bill clients abroad, especially in Europe and the US, and sometimes work with freelancers who bill them in turn. A billable time tracker that handles several currencies and lets freelancers track in the same place as staff keeps all of that in one record, instead of spreading it across spreadsheets and email.
sections.2.heading: Tracking without monitoring your team
sections.2.body:
Many UK firms are wary of time tracking because they associate it with screenshots and activity scores. That's a reasonable concern. The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) published guidance on monitoring workers in 2023. According to [the ICO's announcement](https://ico.org.uk/about-the-ico/media-centre/news-and-blogs/2023/10/ico-publishes-guidance-to-ensure-lawful-monitoring-in-the-workplace), data protection law doesn't prevent monitoring, but monitoring must be necessary and proportionate and must respect workers' rights. Employers are expected to tell workers about the nature, extent and reasons for monitoring, and to use the least intrusive method.

Paidlyo avoids most of that question by design. It records only:

- the hours people enter in the weekly timesheet, or time with the timer;
- the client, project and task they choose;
- whether the time is billable.

It doesn't take screenshots, record apps or websites, or measure keyboard and mouse activity. For a team of professionals, self-reported time is usually all you need to bill accurately and see where time goes.

You should still tell your team why you're tracking time and how the data will be used, for example for client billing, budgets and pricing. Being open about it from the start is good practice, and it helps people record time honestly.
sections.2.callout: Write a short note for the team explaining what's tracked, who sees it and what it's used for. One paragraph prevents most worries.
sections.3.heading: A week of tracking at a London consultancy
sections.3.body:
Here's how a 6-person consultancy in London might use Paidlyo over a typical week.

Each consultant starts the timer when they begin client work, or fills in the weekly timesheet at the end of each day. Entries go against a client, a project and a task, such as research, workshops, reporting or meetings. Internal work, like business development and training, is tracked as non-billable.

Rates are set in pounds on each project: £150 an hour for senior consultants and £95 for analysts, using separate tasks for each level. One client is in Germany, so their project uses euro rates, because Paidlyo sets a currency per client.

By Friday, the hours report shows:

| Category | Hours | Share of the week |
|---|---|---|
| Billable client work | 162 | 72% |
| Business development | 27 | 12% |
| Internal and admin | 36 | 16% |
| Total | 225 | 100% |

That split is useful on its own. If billable time drops below what your pricing assumes, you'll see it within a week, not at the end of the quarter.

At month end, the unbilled time report lists each client's hours, and invoices are created from them in one click, with VAT added where it applies. Our page on [UK invoicing](/invoicing/uk) explains what UK invoices need to show.

sections.5.heading: Pricing, setup and limits
sections.5.body:
Paidlyo costs $9 per person a month, or $90 per person a year, with every feature included and unlimited clients, projects and invoices. Each active person who tracks time is one seat. There's no free plan; the 14-day trial needs a card to start, and nothing is charged until it ends.

Setting up a UK team takes an afternoon:

1. **Add your clients,** with sterling for UK clients and other currencies for clients abroad.
2. **Create projects and tasks** with your rates, and budgets for capped work.
3. **Invite the team** as members, with admins for anyone who manages projects or billing.
4. **Explain what's tracked and why,** in a short note.
5. **Track for a week,** then check the reports and adjust tasks if needed.

If you're moving from Harvest, the CSV importer brings your data across, with a preview before anything is saved.

Limits to know about: Paidlyo has **no mobile apps**, no timesheet approvals, no payroll, no clock-in kiosk and no Xero or QuickBooks integration. It runs in any browser on a computer. Reports export to CSV for your accountant or bookkeeper.

For remote and hybrid teams specifically, see [time tracking for remote teams](/time-tracking/for/remote-teams).

faq.1.question: Does Paidlyo monitor employees?
faq.1.answer: No. Paidlyo records only the time people enter or track with the timer. It takes no screenshots and doesn't record apps or activity.
faq.2.question: Can I track time in pounds and euros?
faq.2.answer: Yes. Rates are set per project, and Paidlyo sets a currency per client.
faq.3.question: Is Paidlyo a working time records system?
faq.3.answer: No. It doesn't record clock-in times or breaks. Check with an HR adviser which working time records you need to keep.
